Cancer. A disease characterized by uncontrolled cell growth and division resulting from mutations that disable tumor suppressors and activate oncogenes, breaking the cell cycle's regulatory checkpoints. Cancer cells lose contact inhibition, evade apoptosis, and proliferate indefinitely, forming tumors that can spread to distant tissues. It ranks among the leading causes of death globally and encompasses over 200 distinct diseases with varying molecular causes, symptoms, and prognoses.

Cancer arises from the accumulation of multiple mutations in a single cell lineage, typically requiring both oncogenic activation and tumor suppressor inactivation. The hallmarks of cancer include unlimited replicative potential, resistance to cell death, sustained proliferation, and the ability to invade and spread to distant sites. These mutations may be inherited or acquired. Environmental factors like smoking, ultraviolet radiation, and viral infection increase mutation rates.

Common origins of cancer include epithelial tissues—which give rise to carcinomas—blood-forming cells, which give rise to leukemias—connective tissues, which give rise to sarcomas—and immune cells, which give rise to lymphomas. Cancer typically requires four to seven key mutations for full malignancy, which explains why cancer incidence increases dramatically with age.

Treatments include surgery, chemotherapy targeting rapidly dividing cells, radiation, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy against specific mutated proteins. Recent advances in immunotherapy exploit cancer cells' ability to hide from immune surveillance, enhancing the immune system's capacity to kill cancer cells. Epigenetic changes can activate cancer genes or silence protective genes without altering the DNA sequences themselves, adding complexity to cancer biology beyond simple mutations.

Cancer heterogeneity—the presence of multiple cell types within a single tumor with different mutations—complicates treatment and drives drug resistance, necessitating combination therapies.
